headline: Brains Bioceutical plans Nasdaq listing via SPAC at $750M valuation
dek: Cannabinoid ingredient maker Brains Bioceutical will merge with Armada Acquisition Corp. III and list on Nasdaq as Brains Therapeutics, ticker BAPI.
key_points: Brains Bioceutical signed a deal on 31 October to merge with the blank-cheque company Armada Acquisition Corp. III at an implied pre-money equity value of about US$750 million.
The combined company would trade on Nasdaq as Brains Therapeutics Corp. under the ticker BAPI, with closing expected in the second quarter of 2027.
Brains makes pharmaceutical-grade cannabinoid ingredients, including CBD, THC and CBN, at a subsidiary's plant in Kent, England, and supplies trial material for an NIH-funded opioid study.
Existing Brains shareholders would roll all their equity into the new company; revenue figures were not disclosed with the announcement.
body: Brains Bioceutical, a Vancouver-headquartered maker of pharmaceutical-grade cannabinoid ingredients, plans to go public on Nasdaq by merging with Armada Acquisition Corp. III, a special purpose acquisition company. The deal, signed on 31 October and announced on 5 November, gives Brains an implied pre-money equity value of approximately US$750 million.

If it closes, the combined business will be called Brains Therapeutics Corp. and trade under the ticker BAPI. Both boards have approved the transaction, which still needs shareholder votes and Nasdaq clearance, and the companies expect to complete it in the second quarter of 2027, according to Business of Cannabis.
## What Brains actually does

Brains is not a grower or a consumer brand. Its business sits further up the pharmaceutical supply chain. A wholly owned subsidiary, BSPG Laboratories, runs an EU-GMP manufacturing facility in Kent, in south-east England, that produces active pharmaceutical ingredients, the purified compounds drugmakers formulate into medicines.

The product list covers CBD, delta-9 THC, delta-8 THC, CBN and CBG, along with drug intermediates and finished medical products. Business of Cannabis reports that the company holds Drug Master Files, Active Substance Master Files and controlled-substance licences across the US, UK, EU, United Arab Emirates, Japan, Australia and Brazil. Those regulatory files are the hard-to-copy part of the business: a drugmaker that wants to use a cannabinoid ingredient in an approved medicine needs a supplier whose manufacturing is already documented with regulators.
The company names no customers, but says its ingredient buyers include one of South America's largest pharmaceutical groups and a major global generics maker.
## The pipeline behind the valuation

A US$750 million price for an ingredient supplier rests heavily on drug development. Brains holds global commercial rights to an extended-release formulation of methazolamide for glaucoma, a non-cannabinoid drug that has cleared a pivotal bioequivalence study under a Special Protocol Assessment agreed with the US Food and Drug Administration.

On the cannabinoid side, Brains supplies clinical trial material to a Phase 3 study of a cannabinoid-based treatment for opioid use disorder. The study is funded by US$18 million from the National Institutes of Health, aims to enrol about 450 people across seven sites, and Brains holds an exclusive option to negotiate a licence to it. The company also lists an oral capsule for epilepsy and an in-house sleep programme.

None of those programmes is yet an approved product, and the announcement did not include revenue or profit figures for Brains. Investors will have to wait for the registration statement that a SPAC merger requires to see audited numbers.
> The pitch is pharma, not cannabis retail: Brains is selling regulatory files and a GMP plant, not a brand.
## The SPAC on the other side

Armada Acquisition Corp. III, chaired by chief executive Stephen Herbert, raised US$248.5 million in a Nasdaq initial public offering that closed in February, selling 24.85 million units at US$10 each. Its shares trade on Nasdaq as AACI. Law firm Morgan Lewis advised Armada III on the Brains deal.

The structure is a full rollover. Existing Brains shareholders are expected to carry 100% of their equity into the combined company rather than cashing out, and Armada III's sponsor and some Brains shareholders have signed support and lock-up agreements. The announcement did not disclose any accompanying private placement. In SPAC deals, the cash that actually reaches the company depends on how many SPAC shareholders choose to redeem their shares for trust cash before closing, so the US$248.5 million raised in February is a ceiling, not a commitment.
## A familiar route with a mixed record

Business of Cannabis describes the deal as the first US public-market debut for a UK-based cannabinoid pharmaceutical manufacturer since Jazz Pharmaceuticals bought GW Pharmaceuticals, maker of the epilepsy drug Epidiolex, in 2021. It also lists earlier cannabis-adjacent SPAC listings: Clever Leaves in December 2020, Weedmaps parent WM Technology in June 2021 and Leafly in February 2022.

Those precedents are a reminder that a SPAC listing is a financing route, not a verdict on value: each of those companies came to market through a shareholder vote on a merger rather than a priced IPO, and the market judged them afterwards.

Brains is arriving at a different moment. In the US, state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved marijuana products moved into Schedule III in April, a shift that puts medical products on a different federal footing from adult-use cannabis. In Europe, Germany's medical market has grown fast since 2024, and Dutch patients have been warned of a supply gap lasting months, both reminders of how much depends on reliable pharmaceutical-grade supply. A supplier with a GMP plant and regulatory files in seven jurisdictions is positioned for buyers who want medicine, not wellness products.
## What to watch

The next milestone is the registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, which should disclose Brains' revenue, margins, customer concentration and the projections behind the US$750 million figure. After that come the Armada III shareholder vote and the redemption level, which will decide how much cash the combined company has on day one. Clinical news on the glaucoma formulation and the NIH-funded opioid study will drive how the market values BAPI after it starts trading, which the companies expect in the second quarter of 2027.
